title: Vayigash: he drew near (Genesis 44:18)
hook: Judah steps forward; the portion's name means "he approached"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph slipped out of the room to cry, washed his face, and walked back in. Your line was wash your face, go back. Today we're still in that room, and someone finally moves.

The silver cup has been found in Benjamin's sack. The brothers have torn their clothes and trudged back to the city. The ruler of Egypt, their brother Joseph, though they still don't know it, gives his verdict: the one with the cup stays here as my slave. The rest of you, go home in peace. Everyone is frozen, like a meeting where the boss has spoken and nobody breathes. It would be easy to look at the floor and let it happen. Then one man steps forward.
screen: `THE CUP IN BENJAMIN'S SACK.` → `THE RULER'S VERDICT.` → `ONE MAN STEPS FORWARD.`

segments.voice: This week's portion is named for its first word, vayigash: and he drew near. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "Then Judah came near unto him." Judah walks up to the man who rules Egypt for Pharaoh, close enough to speak into his ear, and asks to be heard. Remember who Judah is. Years earlier, with Joseph in the pit, it was Judah who said, let's sell him. Now he's the one who won't leave a brother behind. What follows is a long speech. Judah tells the whole story: our old father, the son he lost, the youngest son he barely let us take. If we come home without the boy, our father will die of grief. Then the offer. Keep me instead. Let me stay as your slave, and let the boy go home with his brothers. The rabbis looked hard at that little verb. A midrash says a person can draw near for three reasons: to fight, to make peace, or to pray. Judah, they say, came ready for all three: firm enough to argue, gentle enough to plead, humble enough to hope. The word Jew goes back, through the tribe and later the kingdom of Judah, to his name, Yehudah. In a real sense, the people carry the name of the brother who stepped forward. Before anything in this family can be repaired, somebody has to walk across the room.
screen: `VAYIGASH — AND HE DREW NEAR.` · `JUDAH, WHO ONCE SAID SELL HIM.` · `KEEP ME INSTEAD OF THE BOY.` · `TO FIGHT, TO MAKE PEACE, TO PRAY.` · then, large: `DRAW NEAR.`

segments.voice: Think of a conversation you've been circling: an apology, a request, a talk with someone you love that keeps getting postponed. Picture the room, and yourself taking one step closer. Then choose your first sentence, just the first one, plain and true, and say it silently until it feels like yours.
Vayigash. And he drew near: Judah steps up to the ruler of Egypt and offers himself in place of his youngest brother.
Your line: draw near. The brother who once said sell him now says keep me instead. Day two hundred eleven is yours.

howItsDone: Vayigash is read in synagogue in winter, in early winter; its opening scene of Judah pleading for Benjamin is often taught as the moment the brothers' story turns from betrayal toward repair.

original.note: Hebrew: and he drew near. The first word of the portion, and its name.
